strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding with precise 3D localization, where existing 3DGS-based language-field methods often suffer from semantic bleeding and ambiguous feature assignment.

The main design choice of using an explicit sparse voxel representation for feature fusion is well motivated. The discussion of why disjoint voxel geometry can simplify registration compared with overlapping Gaussians is convincing at a conceptual level.

The empirical results are strong on the reported 3D tasks: LESV improves LERF 3D object retrieval over Dr. Splat and OpenGaussian, and shows a large gain on ScanNet open-vocabulary point cloud understanding across 19/15/10 class settings.

The paper includes useful ablations covering geometry supervision, depth confidence, AM-RADIO features, sliding-window upsampling, and self-correlating aggregation. The efficiency table also supports the claim that feature lifting is substantially faster than mask/distillation-heavy pipelines.
Qualitative examples are aligned with the claimed failure modes, especially reduced spillover and better small-object or part-level retrieval.
weaknesses: The originality is somewhat mixed. Several key components are adopted from prior work: SVRaster, monocular depth/normal regularization, AM-RADIO, and SCRA/SCGA from RADSeg. The contribution is a useful integration, but the paper sometimes presents the resulting pipeline more strongly than the novelty supports.

The experimental protocol needs clearer justification for fairness. For 3D retrieval, the paper changes similarity normalization because AM-RADIO has a different distribution, but it is unclear how thresholds are selected and whether this benefits all methods equally. For ScanNet, feature transfer uses different K values for 3DGS and SVRaster, and Mahalanobis gating is removed based on empirical observations; these choices could materially affect baseline performance.

The claim of state-of-the-art across 2D and 3D benchmarks is overstated. In Table 2, LESV has lower average 2D mIoU than LangSplatV2 and only essentially matches localization accuracy, so the 2D result is competitive rather than clearly SOTA.

Reproducibility details are incomplete. Important hyperparameters such as crop/window size and overlap, Gaussian blending parameters, β/σ values, thresholding strategy, number of views used for fusion, SVRaster training settings, and exact ScanNet/LERF splits are not sufficiently specified in the main paper.

Some technical claims are too strong or insufficiently substantiated. The O(1) memory claim for scalable batch fusion is not convincing as written, since scene storage and feature aggregation still scale with the number of voxels/images even if batching controls peak memory. The deterministic-vs-probabilistic framing also simplifies the fact that voxel rendering and feature fusion still depend on depth estimates, visibility, and confidence weighting.

The ablation table is hard to interpret because the rows appear sequential but mix geometry changes and feature-backbone changes; for example, raw RADIO lowers mIoU but raises Acc@25, sliding-window further lowers mIoU, and the final gain depends heavily on SCRA/SCGA. More isolated ablations would be needed to cleanly attribute improvements.

The paper would benefit from broader evaluation beyond LERF and ScanNet, stronger comparison to recent 2025/2026 baselines where applicable, and reporting variance or per-scene details for the large ScanNet gains. The autonomous-driving examples are interesting but only qualitative, so they do not strongly support the scalability claims.

strengths: The paper targets an important and active problem: open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding with direct 3D querying, where spatial bleeding and multi-scale language grounding are real limitations of existing 3DGS-based approaches.

The proposed combination of an explicit sparse voxel representation, geometric confidence weighting, and dense AM-RADIO features is plausible and well motivated. If validated, the direction could be useful for more deterministic feature fusion and finer 3D localization.

The reported 3D results are strong: LESV improves substantially over Dr. Splat on LERF 3D object retrieval and ScanNet open-vocabulary point cloud segmentation, and the paper includes ablations suggesting that geometry regularization, confidence weighting, and feature refinement each affect performance.
The efficiency motivation is relevant. Avoiding multi-level SAM mask preprocessing and expensive feature distillation is a meaningful practical advantage if the reported timings generalize.
weaknesses: The acceptance case is weakened by serious evaluation and reporting concerns. The paper repeatedly claims state-of-the-art performance across 2D and 3D benchmarks, but Table 2 does not support a 2D SOTA claim: LESV has lower average 2D retrieval mIoU than LangSplatV2 and lower localization than LangSplat, while the text still frames it as SOTA or equivalent.

The evaluation protocol is under-specified and potentially unfair. The authors change thresholding by using normalized cosine similarity because AM-RADIO has different score distributions, but do not explain threshold selection, validation, or whether baselines were retuned comparably. Details such as ScanNet scene selection, query/class prompts, hyperparameters, and exact reproduction settings are missing.

Novelty is limited and somewhat overstated. Much of the method is an assembly of SVRaster, monocular depth/normal regularization, AM-RADIO dense tokens, sliding-window inference, and RADSeg SCRA/SCGA modules. The paper does not clearly separate which parts are genuinely new from borrowed components, nor does it provide enough controlled comparisons to prove the claimed conceptual advances.

Several technical claims are not convincingly justified. The claim of O(1) memory processing regardless of scene scale is especially strong and not supported by analysis or measurements. The deterministic/disjoint voxel argument also does not fully address visibility, occlusion, calibration error, or view-dependent fusion failure modes.

The ablations are insufficient for the scope of the claims. They are mainly sequential on LERF 3D retrieval, making it hard to isolate the effect of SVRaster versus AM-RADIO versus SCRA/SCGA. There is no strong ablation against using the same AM-RADIO features in a Gaussian backbone or the same voxel backbone with alternative dense features.

Reproducibility is poor. Important implementation details are absent or vague, including beta/sigma values, patch sizes, crop/window sizes, RADIO/SigLIP version details, SCRA/SCGA integration, training schedules, thresholds, and hardware specifics beyond an RTX-5090-equivalent GPU. No code or release plan is described.

The manuscript has many polish and consistency problems that undermine confidence: unresolved references such as Figure??, placeholder headers like “Abbreviated paper title,” inconsistent numbers across tables, citation mistakes, typos, and unclear phrases. These are not merely cosmetic because some affect interpretation of results.

The paper lacks a meaningful limitations discussion. Important limitations such as dependence on monocular priors, sensitivity to camera/depth errors, AM-RADIO domain bias, memory scaling with dense features, and failure cases on small or ambiguous objects are not examined. Overall, the work has promising ingredients, but the evidence is not yet reliable enough for acceptance.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and timely contribution for Algorithms/General: replacing unstructured 3D Gaussian primitives with sparse voxel rasterization for language feature fusion, combined with dense AM-RADIO features to reduce multi-level semantic ambiguity. This is a sensible and original system design for open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding.

The technical motivation is strong. The paper identifies concrete failure modes in prior 3DGS language-field registration, especially semantic bleeding and ambiguous feature assignment, and the proposed deterministic voxel fusion directly targets these issues.

Experimental results are compelling across multiple tasks. LESV improves LERF 3D object retrieval over Dr. Splat in average mIoU and Acc@25, substantially improves ScanNet open-vocabulary point cloud segmentation across 19/15/10-class settings, and remains competitive on 2D object retrieval despite not being optimized specifically for that setting.

The ablations are useful and support the main design choices: geometry regularization, depth confidence, AM-RADIO features, sliding-window upsampling, and SCRA/SCGA each affect performance in ways that align with the paper's claims.

The efficiency story is a meaningful strength. The reported reduction in preprocessing and feature lifting time, especially relative to SAM/CLIP mask-based or 3DGS registration pipelines, increases the practical value of the method.

Qualitative results are well chosen and illustrate the claimed benefits on fine-grained and part-level queries, including cases such as object parts, small objects, and reduced spillover at boundaries.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is not yet fully convincing. Important implementation details are under-specified, including exact AM-RADIO variant, feature dimensions, window size/stride, thresholds, confidence bandwidths, TSDF fusion settings, training schedules, memory usage, and whether code/models will be released.

Some evaluation choices could affect fairness. The paper modifies Dr. Splat implementation for memory, changes or normalizes thresholding due to feature-distribution differences, and adapts feature-transfer protocols differently for Gaussian and voxel representations. These may be reasonable, but need more precise justification and sensitivity analysis.

The benchmark coverage is somewhat narrow relative to the broad claims about real-world robotics and autonomous driving. LERF contains only a few scenes, ScanNet is indoor, and KITTI-360 results are qualitative only; stronger outdoor quantitative evaluation would better support the scalability and real-world claims.

The ablation is mostly sequential, so it does not fully disentangle interaction effects among geometry refinement, AM-RADIO features, sliding-window fusion, and SCRA/SCGA. A more factorial ablation or component-isolated comparison would strengthen the causal evidence.

Several claims are phrased too strongly, especially O(1) memory with scene scale and establishing a general foundation for real-world robotic interaction. The reported efficiency numbers are promising but need explicit hardware, peak memory, and scaling curves across scene sizes.

The writing and presentation contain minor but noticeable issues, including placeholder text such as 'Abbreviated paper title', a Figure?? reference, citation/index inconsistencies, and some table formatting problems. These do not undermine the main technical case but should be cleaned up.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding with precise 3D-native localization rather than only feature rendering. The motivation around spatial ambiguity in overlapping 3D Gaussians and semantic dilution from mask-level pooling is clear and relevant.

The proposed system is technically plausible and well aligned with the stated goals. Using SVRaster as a structured voxel backbone, adding monocular depth/normal regularization, and fusing dense AM-RADIO features with geometric confidence is a coherent design that directly targets boundary bleeding and multi-level semantic ambiguity.

The empirical results are promising, especially on ScanNet open-vocabulary point cloud understanding, where the reported gains over Dr. Splat and other 3DGS-based baselines are large across 19/15/10-class settings. The LERF 3D retrieval results are also competitive, with strong Acc@25 and good qualitative examples for small objects and part-level queries.

The paper includes useful ablations that partly disentangle geometry/backbone effects, and the efficiency analysis is valuable. The reported reductions in preprocessing and feature lifting time are practically meaningful for this area, where many methods have heavy SAM/CLIP preprocessing pipelines.
The limitations section is candid about feature upsampling resolution and lack of real-time novel-view feature rendering, which helps calibrate the contribution.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental at the component level. SVRaster, monocular depth/normal supervision, AM-RADIO dense features, and RADSeg-style self-correction are all imported from prior work; the main contribution is their combination and adaptation to language-embedded 3D fusion. This can still be valuable, but the paper should be more precise about what is algorithmically new versus system integration.

The fairness of some comparisons is not fully convincing. The strongest gains come when LESV uses dense AM-RADIO features, while several baselines are tied to SAM+CLIP or mask-pooled variants. The paper argues that Dr. Splat cannot scale to dense AM-RADIO registration, but this is partly an implementation/representation mismatch rather than a controlled comparison. Additional baselines using the same dense feature source in voxel or point-based fusion would strengthen the claim.

Several evaluation protocol choices need more detail and justification: normalized cosine similarity for evaluated methods, altered Dr. Splat memory management, omission of Mahalanobis gating, K choices for feature transfer, and thresholding details. These choices can materially affect open-vocabulary segmentation/retrieval metrics, so reproducibility and fairness are not yet fully established.

The efficiency claims are overstated in places. The paper claims O(1) memory processing regardless of scene scale, but total computation/storage should still depend on the number of voxels, views, and extracted feature maps. The reported peak memory numbers are useful, but the asymptotic statement is not well supported.

The ablations leave some important factors entangled. Table 4 isolates geometry only under SAM+CLIP, and Table 5 shows the full AM-RADIO benefit, but the paper does not fully isolate sliding-window upsampling, SCRA/SCGA, confidence gating, AM-RADIO token choice, crop stride/resolution, and threshold sensitivity in the main experimental section.

The 2D localization/retrieval claims should be toned down. LESV is competitive but not best on average mIoU, and its performance varies substantially by scene, especially on figurines and waldo_kitchen. This does not undermine the 3D-native contribution, but the wording occasionally suggests broader state-of-the-art performance than the tables support.

Implementation details are insufficient for robust reproduction. Important hyperparameters such as beta/sigma values, TSDF fusion settings, crop sizes/overlap, AM-RADIO variant, feature normalization, training schedules for SVRaster refinement, and exact dataset splits/query lists are not clearly specified in the extracted manuscript.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely problem: efficient open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding with direct 3D querying, where current Gaussian-splatting language-field methods do suffer from ambiguity, semantic bleeding, and substantial preprocessing costs.

The proposed direction of using an explicit sparse voxel representation for deterministic feature fusion is sensible, and the paper provides an intuitive explanation for why disjoint voxel geometry could be preferable to overlapping Gaussians for point-level language queries.

The empirical results on ScanNet are potentially interesting: the reported gains over Dr. Splat and other 3DGS-based baselines are large on 19/15/10-class open-vocabulary point-cloud understanding, and the supplementary ScanNet200 result suggests the approach may scale beyond the main 19-class setting.

The paper includes useful ablations separating geometry, monocular/normal supervision, TSDF confidence, and feature backbone effects. It also acknowledges relevant limitations, especially feature upsampling resolution and lack of real-time feature rendering into novel views.
The efficiency motivation is compelling: reducing feature lifting to roughly minutes and avoiding very large memory usage would be practically valuable if reproduced under a clear protocol.
weaknesses: The main scientific case is weakened by the ablations: with identical SAM+CLIP features, replacing Dr. Splat with the proposed SVRaster pipeline gives only very small gains on LERF and ScanNet. The large improvements appear to come primarily from dense AM-RADIO features, while the comparison to Dr. Splat + AM-RADIO is not fully fair because that baseline is forced through mask-level pooling rather than a comparably strong dense-registration variant.

Novelty is incremental and largely compositional. The method combines SVRaster, monocular depth/normal regularization, TSDF confidence, AM-RADIO features, sliding-window inference, and RADSeg-style aggregation. Many core pieces are borrowed, and the paper does not convincingly isolate a new algorithmic insight beyond assembling these components.

Several claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The paper repeatedly claims new state of the art, but on LERF 3D retrieval it is not best in mIoU, and on 2D retrieval it trails Occam's LGS and LangSplatV2 in average mIoU. The text sometimes reframes clearly lower performance as comparable without enough nuance.

Experimental coverage is narrow for some major claims. LERF evaluation covers only four scenes, and the paper does not provide enough detail on ScanNet split size, prompt templates, threshold selection, normalization choices, or whether hyperparameters were tuned per dataset or per scene. This makes the strength of the reported gains hard to judge.

Reproducibility is insufficient. Important implementation details are missing or vague, including crop size/stride for sliding windows, feature-map resolution, exact AM-RADIO/SigLIP head usage, loss weights, beta/sigma values, TSDF construction details from SVRaster, thresholds for cosine similarity, and exact memory-measurement methodology.

The efficiency analysis is not rigorous enough. Hardware is described only as equivalent to an RTX 5090, baseline implementations are modified by the authors, and the preprocessing/fusion/runtime categories are not consistently defined across methods. The O(1) memory claim is especially problematic because memory must still depend on voxel count, feature dimensionality, and batching schedule.

Some comparisons seem potentially unfair or underdeveloped. Baselines optimized for 2D are compared against a method evaluated through 3D projection, while dense AM-RADIO baselines on alternative 3D representations are missing. The paper needs stronger baselines that separate the contribution of the representation from the contribution of the foundation model features.

The method description contains technical ambiguities and some questionable assertions, such as deterministic fusion fully resolving spatial ambiguity and confidence gating being a principled trade-off without deeper theoretical or empirical support. The formulation of multi-level TSDF fusion is mostly relegated to the supplement and remains underspecified.

Presentation quality raises concerns. There are placeholder headers, typos, inconsistent citation labels, duplicated CLIP references, figure-label inconsistencies, and some garbled equations in the manuscript. These issues do not alone determine the score, but they reinforce the impression that the submission is not yet polished enough.

Overall, despite promising empirical signals, the paper does not yet provide a convincing, well-controlled case that the proposed algorithmic contribution, rather than a stronger feature backbone and evaluation choices, is responsible for the headline improvements. I would lean weak reject.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem in open-vocabulary 3D scene understanding: how to build language-aligned 3D feature fields that are spatially precise, efficient, and usable for direct 3D queries.

The core idea of replacing overlapping 3D Gaussians with an explicit sparse voxel representation is well motivated. The deterministic voxel-to-feature fusion directly targets semantic bleeding and ray-like spillover artifacts observed in 3DGS-based language fields.

The method combines several useful components: SVRaster geometry, monocular depth/normal regularization, TSDF-based confidence gating, dense AM-RADIO features, and sliding-window/self-correlating feature aggregation. The resulting system is coherent and practically oriented.

Experimental results are strong, especially on ScanNet open-vocabulary point cloud understanding, where the reported gains over Dr.Splat are large across 19-, 15-, 10-, and 200-class settings. The LERF 3D retrieval and 2D localization results are also competitive, with good qualitative evidence for sharper boundaries and fine-grained part queries.

The ablations are meaningful: the paper separates the effects of geometry refinement, confidence gating, representation choice, and feature backbone. The efficiency analysis is also valuable, showing substantial reductions in preprocessing and feature lifting time compared with several prior pipelines.
The limitations section is candid and useful, especially regarding feature upsampling resolution and the lack of real-time novel-view feature rendering.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat system-level rather than a single sharply new algorithmic insight. Several key ingredients are inherited from recent work: SVRaster, AM-RADIO, RADSeg SCRA/SCGA, monocular depth/normal losses, and TSDF fusion. The contribution is still valuable, but the paper should more crisply distinguish what is newly introduced versus adapted.

Some evaluation choices need clearer justification. For example, the paper uses normalized cosine similarity because AM-RADIO has a different distribution, modifies/optimizes the Dr.Splat implementation, and adapts 2D evaluation for direct registration methods. These may be reasonable, but the fairness and sensitivity of these choices should be documented more thoroughly.

The strongest retrieval baseline, LaGa with multi-level masks, still outperforms LESV in LERF 3D mIoU under its own setting. The paper explains the efficiency tradeoff, but the claim of resolving multi-level ambiguity would be stronger with more direct comparisons under matched compute or matched mask/feature assumptions.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in the main text. Important hyperparameters and implementation choices such as crop size/stride, Gaussian blending parameters, TSDF confidence thresholds, monocular prior model, beta/sigma values, and thresholding protocols appear insufficiently specified for reliable reproduction.

The benchmark scope is solid but still narrow for broad claims: LERF has only a few scenes, ScanNet is indoor-centric, and the KITTI-360 results are qualitative. More diverse real-world scenes or quantitative outdoor evaluation would strengthen the claimed generality.

The manuscript has some presentation issues: tables are crowded and appear to overlap in extraction, terminology is occasionally imprecise, and several references are very recent/preprint/future-dated, which may make attribution and baseline stability harder to assess.
